title: Are there any films that use mixed formats in an interesting/experimental way?

commenti.body: [removed]

in Hirokazu Koreeda’s “Afterlife” (1998), the characters are in a place that resembles limbo. they are the recently deceased and have one week to choose a moment in their lives to remember for the rest of eternity. one of the characters cannot choose so he is given a set of vhs tapes to watch. each tape represents one year in his life. when he pops in a tape, he sees a static shot from what looks like medium-grade security footage: it’s a medium shot of medium distance from its subjects.   he sees his first date with his eventual wife, a moment from his time in college, a moment from his marriage life…all is if they’re on “Candid Camera.”

I’d say animation is probably the easiest starting point… off the top of my head the recent spider-verse movies utilize style changes to help track what worlds we’re on. However there are also interesting “multi-contributor” films like Shrek Retold and Our Robocop remake that recreate the movie in completely different styles from scene to scene, or the Racer Trash radical editing collective that doesn’t actually “remake” the movie in the same way but does stitch together scenes the various members have re-edited in the house style. 

Also, based on what I THOUGHT your question was asking at first, I recommend The Wolf House just because - it’s a really interesting use of mixed media.

There was a British sketch programme in the 90’s called The Fast Show, and one of their recurring characters was a [guy who just walked around discussing things he liked](https://youtu.be/Wv_662IqKto?si=V2P_vZWeGRN436hE). Part of the gag was that each cut would be to a wildly different location, shot on noticeably different gear. Oddly, it pretty accurately predicted YouTube vlogging almost 15 years later, though the creators later admitted in a retrospective they were just trying to be weird and European

And on that note:

Lola Rennt (known as Run Lola Run in English markets) makes use of multiple different formats. I do remember parts shot on film and handheld camcorders, though it’s been a fair few years and I can’t quite remember why.

Dancer In The Dark doesn’t technically play around with formats, but uses radically different set ups and shooting styles to distinguish between reality and fantasy, befitting the films pastiche of musicals.

Flatliners is about a group of medical students who induce near death experiences for science. One character surreptitiously films his various amorous encounters and his sequence is at least semi-diagetically shot to look similar

If…. features multiple, mostly passing and establishing sequences shot in black and white and of a noticeably different grade. Depending on who is giving the interview and at what time this was done for either for aesthetic, technical or budgetary reasons.

The first thing that came to mind was The Florida Project. The ending was shot on an iPhone, which Sean Baker was used to doing since one of his early projects was shot entirely on iPhones (Tangerine). They did it mostly for practical reasons (Disney would never let them film in Disney World) but it also worked narratively since for the first time we're seeing the world from the character's perspective and the shift in camera treatment reflects this shift in perspective.

I suppose the obvious answer is Steve Jobs which is split into three parts, and each section was shot on a different format (16mm, 35mm and digital, respectively) to represent the passage of time and technology. 

See also almost any Michael Mann film from the 2000s, he mixed digital and film formats a lot.

Not a film exactly but the wonderfully shot HBO series Winning Time about the rise of the LA Lakers dynasty uses a ton of different formats including 80s broadcast cameras to achieve the same look of a sports broadcast. They often quickly cut between this, modern footage and what looks to be a mix of super 8/16 etc. 

It is amazing visually.

Aftersun did this brilliantly. They go back and forth between a modern camera and home footage shot on a digital handheld from the early  2000s. It is done digetically and is a big part of the story, but it’s also a powerful symbol of nostalgia and the limitations and blind spots of memory… also the way we investigate and scrutinize our memories as we get older to understand our loved ones who are no longer with us. I say it again the way this is done is absolutely brilliant and everything about this film is so incredible. It is the best movie I’ve ever seen and it’s affected me deeper than any movie ever has.

One of my favorite films. Now need to dig the DVD out of storage to watch it this week.

This is subtle, but the American movie version of State of Play is shot on 35mm with anamorphic lenses for the journalist scenes and the Panavision Genesis with spherical lenses for the politics scenes.

It's quite common in animation to mix styles. Live-action struggles with this (unless there is an animated / comic element such as *300*, *Watchmen* and much of the MCU). For example, *300* uses different colour saturations to show different types of scenes (basically battle and non-battle). 

If you mean using different camera set-ups then I'm not sure. A lot of films use static, portable and/or handheld cameras for different types of scenes but this is typically only done to reflect different styles as such, just to allow different angles and perspectives in shots without having to spend time moving cameras or having to film multiple takes.

Crooklyn uses squeezed anamorphic footage to great effect. There’s also a Sam Fuller film that uses grainy blown up 16mm squeezed anamorphic footage too—one of his pacific theater war films iirc

Harmony Korine does this with *Gummo*, *Julien Donkey-Boy*, and *Spring Breaker*. For example with *Gummo*, he and his editor Christopher Tellefsen mixed Hi-8 videos, polaroid pictures, and 35mm film footages to create this hypnotic stream-of-consciousness feel throughout the movie.

Michael Mann's Blackhat has a crazy mix of formats. Just look at the list of [cameras used!](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2717822/technical/?ref_=tt_spec_sm) He even mixed in some insane GoPro shots.  
  
Bamboozled also mixes Mini DV(all the main narrative) and 35mm (everything from the televised show).
Definitely Super 8. It helped reinvigorate the format.

I havent seen it mentioned, so here I go

In, The Grand Budapest Hotel, Wes Anderson uses different Aspect ratios, based on in which century the story is taking place at the moment.

Not a film but a miniseries, The Virtues (2019) by Shane Meadows (who also directed This is England).

 It uses older cameras that give a 80's/90's home video vibe to show the chracter's childhood flashbacks. I found it really effective in portraying hazy memories. I also consider it a dramatic masterpiece, strongly recommend it.
